What should a founder expect from a CFO at an AI startup?

a16z’s “You Need a New CFO,” by Seema Amble, Ivan Makarov and David Borecky, makes a timely case: finance leaders increasingly design the systems through which the business operates.

My view: that responsibility brings accounting, commercial judgement and product understanding closer together.

The traditional responsibilities remain: reliable accounts, cash discipline, controls and capital allocation. The new mandate is to make them useful at the speed the business moves.

For an AI company, I would start with three questions.
1. Does more usage create more value—or just more cost?
A customer can expand usage while contributing less to the business. I want revenue connected to inference, cloud, implementation and support costs, with the assumptions visible.
That gives founders a basis for deciding which contracts to reprice, which workflows to improve and where growth deserves more investment.
2. Which decisions can an agent make, and who remains accountable?
Before automating a finance workflow, define the evidence required, approval thresholds, exception handling and the person responsible for the outcome.
An agent completing a task is only part of the test. The team must be able to explain and review what happened.
3. What would make us change the plan?
A forecast should help management act when usage, customer commitments or delivery costs change. I would connect those signals to hiring, pricing and spending decisions, with clear triggers for revisiting assumptions.

This is the direction of my work across Actnow, FINANCE KERNEL™ and my theses on AI Cost Governance and Scaling AI Infrastructure from Seed to IPO.

The common thread is building financial foundations around how an AI business actually earns revenue, consumes resources and makes decisions.
My work on finance-agent governance adds another dimension: translating finance judgement into workflows with explicit limits, evidence and human accountability.
After 15+ years across controllership, CFO and finance leadership, I want to bring that experience inside one ambitious AI company and take responsibility for building its next stage.

AI-native founders: which financial decision is hardest today—pricing, compute commitments, funding capacity ahead of demand, or understanding whether growth improves margins?

Investors across VC and PE: what financial capability do you most want your AI portfolio companies to build before their next stage of growth?

I’d welcome your perspectives in the comments. These are also the conversations I’d like to have with founders building their finance leadership team:

Can your business explain how its AI makes decisions that affect people?

From 10 December 2026, Privacy Act changes require APP entities to spell out in their privacy policies when computer programs use personal information to make — or substantially help make — decisions that could significantly affect someone's rights or interests. Think hiring, lending, pricing, or customer outcomes. That mainly covers organisations with annual turnover above $3 million, plus some others regardless of size.

The trap for smaller teams is shadow AI. A Conga survey of 1,500 business leaders found one in five didn't know whether their contract or quoting systems already had AI built in. If you can't see it, you can't document it.

Practical moves before December:
• Map where AI and automation shape decisions that use personal data
• Make sure those processes are visible and auditable — black boxes won't pass
• Update your privacy policy so it matches what actually happens

The conversation around Spark optimization in 2026 has moved past shuffle tuning and partition sizing. Those are table stakes, automated by the engine itself. The real frontier is understanding how Spark's optimizer interacts with the new generation of data sources that do not follow the traditional HDFS or cloud storage patterns.

The most non-obvious insight I have encountered this year is that the costliest performance problems in PySpark are no longer computational; they are semantic. As Apache Spark 4.2.0 matures, its cost-based optimizer becomes increasingly sophisticated, but it still cannot infer the intent of your transformation. I am seeing teams that spend hours optimizing a join that should have been a merge in the first place, or debugging a spill that is actually the result of a poorly designed data contract, not a resource allocation problem.

The seven optimization tips that emerged in 2026 all converge on a single principle: the fastest Spark job is the one that does the least unnecessary work. But what constitutes "unnecessary" has changed. With the rise of agentic AI workloads that self-modify pipelines, the optimization target is no longer a single job. It is the system's ability to maintain predictable performance under schema drift, cost anomalies, and governance enforcement without human intervention.

Another structural shift is the decoupling of compute and storage in the lakehouse, which means the bottleneck is no longer disk I/O but the metadata layer. I have observed that teams who pre-materialize statistics and histogram data in Unity Catalog reduce query planning time by 60%. The optimization that matters most is not at the execution level but at the planning level, where the engine decides what to read.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to tune Spark shuffle partitions or rewrite PySpark UDFs in Scala. I am seeking a problem where I can design the optimization frameworks and semantic validation layers that make PySpark predictable for agentic, real-time workloads. If your team is struggling with Spark jobs that degrade unpredictably under schema evolution, or with cost spikes from unnecessary data scans caused by poor query planning, I want to hear about the specific workload patterns and latency targets you are facing.

What is the one Spark optimization technique that, if automated at the planning stage, would eliminate your most common performance regression?

Indian IT just shrank for the first time in twenty years.
In the same year, its AI hiring grew 16%.

TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Tech Mahindra ended FY26 with 7,389 fewer people between them. TCS alone is cutting about 12,000 roles, mostly in middle and senior management.

Meanwhile, AI-related IT hiring rose 16% year on year in June, while overall IT hiring fell 3%.

Both numbers are true at once. The pricing model explains why.

For thirty years, most IT contracts were time and materials. The client paid per person per month. More people meant more revenue, so the org chart was a pyramid: many freshers at the base, managers above them, a few leaders on top.

Now clients want to pay for outcomes. Tickets closed. Migrations done. Invoices processed. The vendor is paid for the result, however many people it took.

Under that contract, every extra head eats the margin. The roles that existed mainly to supervise headcount get squeezed first. So does the entry-level work an agent can now do.

What grows is the middle: engineers who can build the AI, run it inside a client's systems and fix it when it breaks.

The pyramid is turning into a diamond.

If you work in IT services, the useful question is what your contract pays for. If it pays for hours, the pressure is coming. If it pays for results, the people who deliver them are the ones being hired.

Time and materials built the pyramid.
Outcomes are building the diamond.

NO JOB AFTER A DEGREE? INDIA’S ENTRY-LEVEL WORKFORCE IS FACING A NEW AI REALITY.
 
 
 
For millions of Indian students, graduating from college has traditionally been the beginning of a corporate career. But that first step is becoming harder as AI takes over routine work that once provided freshers with their entry point into the workforce.
 According to India Today, companies are increasingly using AI for tasks such as checking documents, processing loans, reconciling accounts, preparing invoices and writing basic code. As these tasks become automated, graduates are competing for fewer traditional entry-level opportunities.
 
The shift is already visible at major IT services companies. India Today reports that Infosys terminated contracts of hundreds of trainees last year, while TCS announced plans to cut 12,000 jobs worldwide, mostly in India. Major IT companies also added only 17 net employees during the first nine months of the current financial year, according to an ING research note cited by the report.
 
This creates a difficult cycle for fresh graduates. Companies increasingly want people who understand AI, cloud computing, cybersecurity or machine learning - and who can connect those technologies to real business problems. But graduates often need their first job to gain that experience.
 
The definition of an “entry-level” candidate is changing. Knowing how to code may no longer be enough. Employers increasingly need people who understand how AI systems work, can evaluate their outputs, recognise their limitations and know when human judgement is required.
 
AI is also changing team sizes. Lalit Ahuja, CEO of ANSR, told Bloomberg that a technology programme that previously required about 50 engineers over a year can now be completed by four to 10 people in roughly four weeks with AI.
 That does not automatically mean mass unemployment. It means companies can become more selective, hiring fewer people for routine work while placing greater value on specialized skills.
 
The bigger issue is the disappearing first rung of the career ladder. If AI performs the routine tasks that once helped graduates learn on the job, companies and students may need a different path into employment - one built around real projects, apprenticeships, AI literacy and demonstrable skills.
 
A degree can open the door. But in an AI-driven labour market, proof of what you can actually do may determine whether that door opens.

**You can't create a skilled IT workforce overnight simply by restricting access to foreign talent.**

The US Department of Labor has announced the suspension of Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini from its Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme.

This freezes a key part of the employment-based green card process for these companies.
Having worked with many of these organisations over the last 15 years, this news caught my attention.

Earlier in my career, I was heavily involved in bringing Indian IT professionals into Southeast Asia, including placing engineers and technical specialists on contract assignments with multinationals such as ExxonMobil.

One thing became very clear.

**India has been one of the world's most important sources of skilled IT talent for decades.**

Not simply because of cost, but because of the sheer depth and scale of its technology workforce.

In countries like Thailand, finding experienced professionals in specialised areas of IT has always been a challenge. Sometimes the local talent simply isn't available.

Indian professionals have helped bridge that gap, supporting enterprise systems, infrastructure and major technology transformation projects.

I understand the argument for protecting domestic employment. Companies should absolutely invest in developing local talent.

But there's a difference between hiring overseas workers to reduce costs and hiring internationally because the required skills genuinely aren't available.

Look at Thailand today.

We're attracting investment in data centres, cloud infrastructure, AI and advanced technology. Yet experienced technical professionals remain in short supply.

These skills take years to develop.

And as AI accelerates technological change, the gap between what businesses need and what local talent markets can provide could become even wider.

The US restrictions target permanent labour certification, not international outsourcing as a whole. But they raise a bigger question about the future of global technology recruitment.

Will companies invest more in domestic talent? Will they expand offshore delivery? Or will specialised international talent become even more valuable?

Perhaps India's role as a global technology talent hub isn't coming to an end. Maybe the location where Indian engineers deliver their work will simply change.

My view is that developing local capability and accessing international expertise aren't mutually exclusive.

**You can restrict the movement of people. You can't legislate a skills shortage out of existence.**

Interested to hear how others in technology and recruitment see this developing.

What should we watch next?

Future US policy decisions, outsourcing contracts, company earnings and actual hiring trends will reveal whether this remains an immigration issue or develops into a broader business challenge.

My perspective: This is a signal to monitor, not a reason to panic. The real concern is whether changing US policies eventually influence how much work American clients outsource to India.

From Side Hustle to Solo Unicorn: The OPC Era has arrived
How a single shareholder with AI agents can now build, scale and sell a real business in ~10 months instead of 3 years.

1) What is OPC?
OPC (One Person Company) is a limited liability company with a single shareholder. It has its own legal identity, and the owner’s risk is capped at the capital they put in, so personal assets are protected. I learned that this legal boundary is what separates an OPC from a sole proprietorship:
Sole proprietorship: unlimited liability, hard to finance, best for low-cost 0→1 experiments and side hustles.
OPC: limited liability, bankable and acquirable, built for scaling 1→100 and serving corporate clients.
The rule of thumb
When monthly revenue is stable and clients start asking for invoices and corporate contracts, it’s time to upgrade to transform.

2) Why OPC now 2026, and how did it evolve?
In 2026 golden era, I learned that powered by AI, the OPC is no longer a “small but beautiful” compromise. It’s becoming a formal business asset that can be financed, traded and passed on. It evolved in clear stages:
• Before 2023, gig economy: drivers, couriers and online shop owners trading time for money.
• 2023–2025, AI-augmented individuals: using ChatGPT and Midjourney to multiply income 5–10x.
• 2026, the OPC: compliance, risk isolation and asset-based operations.
• 2027+, micro-multinationals: reaching global customers through FBA, Stripe, AWS and APIs.
• 2030, the $1B “solo unicorn”: the “10-person unicorn” becomes a repeatable path.
I learned that AI compresses the startup lifecycle from quarters to weeks. Idea → MVP → Launch → Scale shrinks from about 3 years to about 10 months, and one founder with a set of agents can now complete the first three stages.

3) What are the characteristics of an OPC?
• The first characteristic is ultimate personalization.
OPCs serve niche needs that big companies ignore because of the “scale trap,” and the workflow adapts to the founder, not the other way round.
• The second is silicon-based production.
The model is no longer humans hiring humans but humans hiring digital employees, so organizational structures get overlapped, compressed and reorganized.
• The third is liquid capabilities.
Founders no longer have glaring weaknesses, because AI raises every “valley” in their skill curve above the bar for delivering work, and the cost of acquiring a new skill approaches zero.

The two human skills remain core:
Inquiry: turning a vague vision into precise instructions AI can execute.
Taste: judging what’s good, which AI can’t replace.
I learned that the bottleneck is no longer what you can build, but what you choose to build.

References : Anthropic’s 《Founder’s Handbook》, Tsinghua OPC Report (2026)

LinkedIn Post: Two Days at Atlassian
Two days. Two very different events. Both at Atlassian's Sydney office. Both changed how I think about what's ahead.
On Tuesday evening I was at the Cursor Meetup Sydney, hosted on Level 29 of Atlassian's George St building. Builders, designers, and engineers in one room talking about what's actually being shipped with AI tooling right now. Not theory. Not hype. Real workflows.

Then on Wednesday I came back for a MechSoc x ActivateUTS site visit, where a panel of Atlassian grads and engineers sat down with us and got real about what working in tech actually looks like in 2026.

Three things stuck with me:
1. The job has flipped. One of the biggest takeaways from the panel was how much AI has changed the development workflow. Engineers are spending more time reviewing generated code, understanding systems, and correcting what AI gets wrong.

One senior engineer made a point that stood out to me: agent-generated architecture still requires human judgement and correction.
It reinforced something important: using AI to produce code is one thing. Understanding whether that code is actually good, maintainable, and right for the user is another.

2. Communication is becoming the real technical skill. This one hit home. As AI speeds up the code side of things, the friction that remains is between people. Contracts don't match because teams didn't talk. A designer wants one thing, an engineer built another. Multiple panelists said that communication skills are increasingly what recruiters and hiring managers are looking for. Not just how well you code, but how well you explain, collaborate, and navigate decisions with people from different crafts.
3. Nobody has all the answers. That's the point. Every single person on that panel, from fresh grads to a senior engineer with years of experience, said the same thing in different words: they're all figuring it out. The problems are undefined. The systems are complex. And the culture at Atlassian seems built around that reality. Blameless incident reviews. A fail-fast approach where you build something in a week and reflect on why it did or didn't work. And mentors who genuinely want you to grow, not just perform.

I walked out of both days reminded that curiosity and the willingness to learn will always matter more than having the answers upfront. The industry is moving fast, but the people who stay curious, communicate well, and aren't afraid to be wrong are the ones who'll keep up.

Grateful for the experience. Big thanks to MechSoc and ActivateUTS for organising the site visit, and to the Atlassian team for being so open with us.

Mark Cuban argues that the corporate anxiety surrounding artificial intelligence eliminating jobs is misplaced. Instead of AI, he highlights that skyrocketing healthcare costs are the hidden burden driving corporate layoffs and hiring freezes.

• Employers frequently blame AI for staff reductions because it serves as an easier scapegoat than facing systemic business issues.

• Rather than fearing AI as a job killer, Cuban advises executives to actually utilize tools like ChatGPT or Claude to audit their healthcare insurance policies and pinpoint exactly where they are overpaying.

The US workforce conversation is changing — and IT staffing will have to change with it.

The recent suspension of PERM processing involving several major technology companies like TCS, Infosys, HCL and others is another signal that the US is taking a closer look at how companies build their technology workforce.

But I think the bigger question is not simply H-1B vs. US talent.
It is "How do companies build the right technology workforce when skills are changing faster than traditional hiring models?"

AI, cloud, cybersecurity, data engineering and digital transformation are creating demand for highly specialized talent. At the same time, organizations are facing greater pressure around workforce compliance, cost, speed and access to talent.

This could accelerate a few trends:
• Greater demand for US work-authorized technology talent
• More focus on skills-based hiring rather than location-based hiring
• Increased adoption of contract, SOW and project-based workforce models
• Greater use of AI to augment—not simply replace—technology talent
• More strategic partnerships between employers, MSPs and staffing providers

For staffing companies like ours, this is a reminder that the value proposition cannot simply be “we can find you people.”

The real value is helping organizations answer:
What skills do we need? Where can we find them? What workforce model makes sense? And how quickly can we deploy them?

The future of IT staffing may be less about filling requisitions and more about designing the workforce needed to execute the business strategy.

That is a conversation I believe employers, MSPs and staffing leaders should be having now. Let me know in the comments what you think of this step taken by the US.

Saw this one from The Hacker News and it’s wild. Researchers built a fake crypto startup, posted developer jobs, and hired three people through a totally normal interview process. All three turned out to be suspected North Korean IT workers running fake identities.

One sent a driver’s license that Google’s own tools flagged as AI generated. Another used a real person’s ID with a swapped photo. They passed interviews, signed contracts, got company laptops... normal hiring, start to finish. Nobody caught it at the interview because nobody was actually checking who was on the other end of the camera.

This is exactly why we built 909Shield. If verification only happens once, on day one, and it’s just “does this ID look real”, you’re trusting a process that’s already been beaten in the wild. Verify the actual person; at the interview and every time it matters after, not just at the paperwork stage.
